hero.title: About Velxio
hero.subtitle: A free, open-source embedded systems emulator — built by a single developer with a passion for hardware and open source.

story.heading: The Story
story.p1: Velxio started as a personal exploration into how microcontroller emulators work internally — CPU instructions, memory management, peripheral timing, and low-level architecture. What began as a learning project during a vacation quickly grew into something bigger.
story.p2: The idea was simple: what if anyone could simulate Arduino, ESP32, and Raspberry Pi boards directly in the browser, without buying hardware, without installing toolchains, without cloud accounts?
story.p3: Velxio v1 launched on Product Hunt and Hacker News, supporting Arduino Uno and Raspberry Pi Pico. The feedback from the maker and embedded community was incredible — and it pushed the project forward.
story.p4: Velxio 2.0 shipped with ESP32 emulation via QEMU (using the lcgamboa fork), a Raspberry Pi 3 running real Linux, RISC-V support for ESP32-C3 and CH32V003, realistic sensor simulation (DHT22, HC-SR04, WS2812B NeoPixel), and 19 boards across 5 CPU architectures — all running real compiled code.
story.p5: The v2 launch hit the front page of Hacker News for over 20 hours, reaching nearly 600 GitHub stars and thousands of visitors in less than 24 hours. It's now being used by students, professors, and makers around the world.

howItWorks.heading: How It Works
howItWorks.avrRp2040Body: Cycle-accurate emulation runs entirely in your browser using avr8js and rp2040js. No backend needed for simulation.
howItWorks.esp32Body: Xtensa ESP32 and ESP32-S3 run on backend QEMU (lcgamboa fork) with real flash images, GPIO, ADC, and timers.
howItWorks.riscvBody: ESP32-C3 (DevKit, XIAO, SuperMini) and CH32V003 are emulated through the QEMU lcgamboa fork with libqemu-riscv32, the same backend pattern as Xtensa ESP32.
howItWorks.raspiBody: Full ARM Cortex-A53 Linux via QEMU raspi3b — boots real Raspberry Pi OS and runs Python with RPi.GPIO.

openSource.heading: Open Source Philosophy
openSource.lead: Velxio is 100% open source under the AGPLv3 license. No cloud dependency, no student accounts, no data leaving your network. Universities and bootcamps can deploy it on their own servers with a single Docker command and give every student access to a complete embedded development environment — for free.
openSource.creditsIntro: The project builds on top of amazing open-source work from the community:

credits.qemuLcgamboa: ESP32 and Raspberry Pi QEMU emulation

openSource.inspiredBy: Velxio was inspired by Wokwi, which is a fantastic tool. The goal of Velxio is to take a different path: fully open source, self-hostable, and supporting multiple heterogeneous boards in the same circuit.

creator.heading: The Creator
creator.bio1: Application Architect with over 10 years of experience leading the development of large-scale enterprise ecosystems. Specialist in Generative AI (LLMs, RAG, LangChain), Cloud-Native architectures (OpenShift, Kubernetes), and certified Odoo ERP expert. Currently at IBM working on enterprise applications for the Uruguayan State Insurance Bank (BSE).
creator.bio2: Studied Computer Science Engineering at Universidad de Oriente in Cuba (2012-2017), then moved to Uruguay where he built a career spanning roles at Quanam (Odoo implementations for government institutions), and IBM (enterprise architecture for BPS and BSE).
creator.bio3: Programming and robotics enthusiast. Creator of other open-source projects including a 3D racing game running on an ESP32 (viral on Reddit with 40K+ views) and an iPod Classic clone for Raspberry Pi.

releases.heading: Recent releases
releases.v3Tagline: Retro CPUs, multi-board systems, full-circuit accuracy
releases.v3Blurb: Programmable Z80/8080/4004 retro CPUs with custom ROM, MicroSD and ePaper emulation, true multi-board UART/I2C/SPI interconnect, ESP32-CAM, full undo/redo, the complete ngspice WASM migration, an 88% smaller bundle, and 100+ new examples.
releases.v25Tagline: Arduino meets SPICE in your browser
releases.v25Blurb: Real-time analog circuit simulation via ngspice-WASM, wired to Arduino, ESP32 and Raspberry Pi Pico. 100+ SPICE-accurate components, live ammeters and voltmeters, 40 new analog/hybrid examples — co-simulated with your firmware.
releases.v2Blurb: Full QEMU-driven ESP32 emulation with WiFi/BLE, Raspberry Pi 3B Linux, MicroPython support across Pico/ESP32, custom WASM chips, and a redesigned canvas with multi-board co-simulation.

quote.p1: "I studied Computer Science in Cuba from 2012 to 2017, and when I moved to Uruguay, the most common question was: 'How did you graduate as an engineer without internet, without a computer, without YouTube?'
quote.p2: I only had 4 words for the answer: Perseverance! Perseverance! Perseverance! Perseverance!
quote.p3: There is no better motivation than not having a plan B."

imageToCode.title: Image to C array for OLED displays
imageToCode.intro: Drop in a picture and get a monochrome C byte array you can paste straight into an Arduino sketch. Tune the threshold and dithering, then check the result on a simulated 128x64 SSD1306 before you flash it.
imageToCode.dropTitle: Drop an image, or click to choose one
imageToCode.dropHint: PNG, JPG, GIF, BMP, WebP or SVG. You can also paste one with Ctrl+V.
imageToCode.errorDecode: Could not read that image. Try a PNG or JPG.
imageToCode.errorCopy: Clipboard blocked. Select the code and copy it manually.
imageToCode.backgroundHint: Fills padding and shows through transparent pixels.
imageToCode.thresholdHint: Pixels brighter than this are lit on the display.
imageToCode.drawHorizontalHint: One bit per pixel, most significant bit first, each row padded to a whole byte. This is what display.drawBitmap() expects.
imageToCode.drawVerticalHint: One byte per column per 8-row page, bit 0 at the top. This is the raw SSD1306 display buffer layout.
imageToCode.oledHint: The bitmap is centred on the panel, exactly as the simulator would render it.
imageToCode.outputPlaceholder: Add an image to generate the array.
